brief: Why side projects outlive the jobs that funded them

slots.eyebrow: On the work nobody asked for
slots.subtitle: Six things that decide whether the thing you make on Saturdays is still worth something in five years.
slots.item1: Why the freedom that starts them also kills them
slots.item2: The only return that is actually guaranteed
slots.coverNote: The last page is the one survivorship hides

slots.body: Nobody scoped it, nobody is waiting for it, and there is no version of it that gets rejected in review. That is the entire appeal, and it is also why so many die in week three — the same absence of pressure that made it possible makes it optional.
slots.p1Body: The only project where you get to decide what good means.
slots.p2Body: Which is the same fact, and it is what kills most of them.
slots.p3Body: One person expecting it is enough. Two is a job.

slots.body: The value is rarely the thing itself. It is that you tried a way of working, a tool or a subject at full scale without anybody's money on it, and that experience transfers whole into work that does have money on it.
slots.p1Title: Try the method, not the idea
slots.p1Body: Pick it because of how you will have to work, not what it is.
slots.p2Body: An unfinished experiment teaches you almost nothing.
slots.p3Body: The point is the next project, not this one.

slots.body: Roles disappear, companies pivot, and the thing you shipped inside one becomes impossible to show or explain. A project with your name on it is the only portfolio that survives an employer, which is why it compounds and salaried work does not.
slots.p1Body: Nothing internal can be shown, five years later, to anybody.
slots.p2Body: People understand a finished thing faster than a job title.
slots.p3Body: Long after you have stopped touching it.

slots.body: Nobody abandons a project because it was too easy. They abandon it because the finished version was three months away and nothing shippable existed at any point before that, so there was never a moment when stopping felt like completing.
slots.p1Body: Not a plan for a week. A thing that exists in a week.
slots.p2Body: Embarrassment is a much stronger schedule than intention.
slots.p3Body: A small good thing beats a large abandoned one.

slots.body: The hours come from somewhere, and pretending otherwise is how people burn a year and resent it. Treating it as leisure is honest; treating it as an investment that must return turns the one unpressured thing you have into another job.
slots.p1Body: Two evenings, or a Saturday morning. Not whatever is left.
slots.p2Body: A project that eats your recovery is a project that ends badly.
slots.p3Body: That is the licence the whole thing runs on.

slots.body: Survivorship makes this look like a reliable strategy, and it is not. The overwhelming majority are abandoned, ignored, or good and unnoticed, and the ones you have heard about are the exception being described as the method.
slots.p1Body: Do it because the making is worth the hours on its own.
slots.p2Body: That return is guaranteed. No other return is.
slots.p3Body: The compounding is across projects, not inside one.

slots.body: Not the one you designed. Whatever part of it could exist by Sunday and be shown to one person without an explanation attached.
slots.closingLine: Finished and small compounds. Ambitious and abandoned teaches you the same lesson every time.
slots.signoff: The rehearsal is the whole return
